prize_parts.citation: For firm-heterogeneity models of trade that explain exporter selection, reallocation across firms and new channels for the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: B010 is the candidate where I see the best combination of a clear conceptual advance, testable predictions and a long record of confirmation. Melitz (2003) moved trade theory from representative industries to firms that differ in productivity. That yields sharp predictions about who exports, how exporter premia arise and why trade liberalisation reallocates activity toward more productive firms. These predictions have been tested on firm-level data in many countries, which is the kind of evidence I weigh most heavily. Helpman's broader theory of trade with differentiated products and firms, including the exporting-versus-FDI work with Melitz and Yeaple, widens the contribution beyond one paper. The framework is now standard in teaching and in trade-policy evaluation, and more than two decades of extension give it ample maturity. The two-name attribution is also comparatively clean. All eleven openings ranked B010 first, second or third in ten cases, so the breadth of support across different fields is a useful signal. I treat that as a reason to scrutinise the candidate carefully and not as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that the headline quantitative claims depend on parametric assumptions, notably Pareto productivity draws, so the size of the selection gains from trade is less settled than the qualitative mechanism. Attribution is also not fully clean. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are important empirical and theoretical precursors who are not credited on this ballot, and Redding's quantitative extensions are left out of a two-name proposal. The committee would have to defend that boundary. Finally, trade was recognised in 2008, so the committee must be satisfied that this is a distinct advance and not a continuation of earlier work. My assessment rests on my own background knowledge, and I have not independently verified the record.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B010 sixth and asks whether it is a distinct advance beyond the new trade theory recognised in 2008. He ranks the Kiyotaki-Moore credit-cycles mechanism first as a conceptually foundational idea.
responses.response: I take the Krugman question seriously, but I think the answer is that it is distinct. The 2008 work explained intra-industry trade with representative firms and scale economies. Melitz changes the unit of analysis to the firm and generates selection, exporter premia and reallocation gains. These are new and separately testable predictions that firm-level data could confirm or reject. That is what makes the contribution a discovery and not a refinement. I agree with him that B019 is conceptually foundational, and I rank it second. I would still put B010 first because its predictions have been confronted with data across many countries, whereas direct identification of the collateral-amplification channel is harder than the theory's influence suggests. I also note his disclosed collaboration with Klenow on B013, which does not affect B010 or B019.

responses.point: Hassler also ranks B010 first with Helpman and Melitz. He cautions that Eaton-Kortum and the Bernard-Jensen exporter-premium pioneers sit outside the credited names, and that Helpman might be seen as better matched to a broader trade-lifetime framing.
responses.response: I agree on the pairing and on the attribution risk, and I do not want to paper over it. The Bernard-Jensen exporter facts were an important empirical anchor, and Eaton-Kortum is a parallel route into quantitative trade. The citation should therefore be narrow: selection, reallocation and the gains from trade in firm-heterogeneity models. It should not claim all of modern trade. That wording keeps the focus on Melitz, with Helpman's firm-level and FDI work, and keeps Eaton-Kortum for a separate discussion alongside B043 if the committee wishes. I would resist a lifetime-achievement framing for Helpman. It would weaken the specific, testable-discovery case that I consider the strongest argument for this candidate.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B037 first. He argues that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford capture the pricing mechanism, the policy rule and the integrated framework, and that the New Keynesian apparatus is used daily in central banks.
responses.response: I accept that the policy influence is very large and that the three names map onto distinct components. My difficulty is that the credit is spread across a literature including Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others, so any three-person cut leaves out serious claimants. Several members, including Krusell himself, name this as the main weakness. The framework's performance in the 2021-23 inflation is also debated, and I would want that assessed before treating the baseline as settled. I would not call this a reason to exclude B037 from consideration. Compared with B010, though, it is a synthesis of many contributions, and B010 is one discovery with a short and defensible list of credited names.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B019 first and proposes adding Gertler, because the financial accelerator is the other half of the credit-friction paradigm. He acknowledges the overlap with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: I see the logic, since the two strands are complementary. I would still keep the credit to Kiyotaki and Moore. The accelerator strand overlaps most directly with Bernanke's 2022 recognition, which makes the boundary hard to draw. Gertler also appears on B037, so adding him creates credit overlap across ballot entries that the committee would have to resolve. If the committee prefers the broader grouping, B019 remains my first alternative. Even then, I would want its empirical identification discussed more explicitly than the theory's influence alone would suggest.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a two-name B010 citation without Redding, or without Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and how it would justify that boundary.
How sensitive the quantitative gains-from-trade results are to parametric assumptions such as Pareto productivity draws, and whether this weakens the case.
Whether the committee sees B010 as clearly distinct from the 2008 recognition of new trade theory.
Whether the empirical identification of the collateral-amplification channel in B019 is strong enough to rank it above B010 on evidential grounds.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My documented connections (Brodeur, Rand, Fudenberg, Nowak, Camerer, Johannesson and others) do not include any credited name on B010, B019 or B001. I have not independently verified this beyond the profile.
